chief_complaint: pain behind my left eye when looking around and blurred vision for 4 days
hpi_details: 4-day history of progressive blurring and dimness of vision in her left eye, accompanied by a sharp, aching pain deep behind the globe that characteristically worsens during eye movements. Noticed that red colours look washed out or grey when viewed with her left eye alone. Also reports an electric shock-like sensation running down her spine into her legs when she bends her neck forward (Lhermitte's phenomenon). Recalls an episode 1 year ago where her right leg felt numb and tingling for 3 weeks, which resolved without medical attention.
ideas: thinks she strained her optic nerve from working long hours on computer screens
concerns: terrified she will go completely blind in both eyes at a young age
expectations: wants urgent eye steroid drops and an MRI scan to check her optic nerve and brain
pmh: episode of unexplained right lower limb numbness 1 year ago lasting 3 weeks, mild vitamin D deficiency

clinical_knowledge.topic: Multiple Sclerosis (Relapsing-Remitting, presenting with optic neuritis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Multiple Sclerosis (Relapsing-Remitting, presenting with optic neuritis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Admit or arrange urgent outpatient neurology treatment for acute relapse: high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 to 5 days (or oral bioequivalent) combined with gastroprotection (PPI) to shorten recovery duration of optic neuritis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: pain behind my left eye when looking around and blurred vision for 4 days

Key HPI features: 4-day history of progressive blurring and dimness of vision in her left eye, accompanied by a sharp, aching pain deep behind the globe that characteristically worsens during eye movements. Noticed that red colours look washed out or grey when viewed with her left eye alone. Also reports an electric shock-like sensation running down her spine into her legs when she bends her neck forward (Lhermitte's phenomenon). Recalls an episode 1 year ago where her right leg felt numb and tingling for 3 weeks, which resolved without medical attention.

Objective/Exam findings: Visual acuity: reduced in left eye (e.g., 6/36) vs normal right eye (6/6). Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) positive on swinging flashlight test. Fundoscopy: normal optic disc initially (retrobulbar neuritis: 'the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing') or mild disc swelling. Check red desaturation with red hat pin. Neurological exam: brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilateral positive Babinski signs. MRI Brain and Cervical Spine with gadolinium contrast (reveals multiple periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial ovoid T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter lesions oriented perpendicular to ventricles - Dawson's fingers). Lumbar puncture for CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands positive in CSF but absent in matched serum).
Relevant background/PMH: episode of unexplained right lower limb numbness 1 year ago lasting 3 weeks, mild vitamin D deficiency
Current medications: vitamin D3 1000 IU OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Multiple Sclerosis (Relapsing-Remitting, presenting with optic neuritis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Neuromyelitis optica (NMO/Devic's disease) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Complete vision loss or bilateral involvement — would suggest a more severe or different demyelinating process.
management_principles: Admit or arrange urgent outpatient neurology treatment for acute relapse: high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 to 5 days (or oral bioequivalent) combined with gastroprotection (PPI) to shorten recovery duration of optic neuritis
Urgent referral to MS specialist clinic for initiation of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs - e.g., natalizumab, ocrelizumab, or fingolimod) to prevent future relapses and disability accumulation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29F presents with acute left optic neuritis (pain on eye movement, visual loss, red desaturation), positive Lhermitte's phenomenon, and prior episode of self-resolving sensory disturbance separated in time and space.
reference_soap.objective: Visual acuity: reduced in left eye (e.g., 6/36) vs normal right eye (6/6). Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) positive on swinging flashlight test. Fundoscopy: normal optic disc initially (retrobulbar neuritis: 'the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing') or mild disc swelling. Check red desaturation with red hat pin. Neurological exam: brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilateral positive Babinski signs. MRI Brain and Cervical Spine with gadolinium contrast (reveals multiple periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial ovoid T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter lesions oriented perpendicular to ventricles - Dawson's fingers). Lumbar puncture for CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands positive in CSF but absent in matched serum).
reference_soap.assessment: Multiple Sclerosis - Relapsing-Remitting subtype (RRMS) presenting with acute left optic neuritis. Satisfies McDonald diagnostic criteria for dissemination in time and space. DDx: neuromyelitis optica (NMO / Devic's disease - check anti-AQP4 antibodies), MOG-antibody disease, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), neurosarcoidosis.
reference_soap.plan: Admit or arrange urgent outpatient neurology treatment for acute relapse: high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 to 5 days (or oral bioequivalent) combined with gastroprotection (PPI) to shorten recovery duration of optic neuritis. Urgent referral to MS specialist clinic for initiation of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs - e.g., natalizumab, ocrelizumab, or fingolimod) to prevent future relapses and disability accumulation. Ophthalmology consult.

learning_objectives: Elicit classical features of optic neuritis including pain exacerbated by eye movements and red colour desaturation
Recognise Lhermitte's phenomenon and correlate historical transient neurological episodes with dissemination in time and space
Perform pupillary examination identifying a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) via swinging flashlight test
Explain the acute relapse management protocol (high-dose IV methylprednisolone) and the long-term necessity of Disease-Modifying Therapies

teaching.diagnosis: Multiple Sclerosis (Relapsing-Remitting, presenting with optic neuritis)
teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune attack on the myelin sheath of the optic nerve causing painful vision loss (worse with eye movement, colors look washed out) — a prior unexplained episode of limb numbness a year ago satisfies the 'dissemination in time and space' needed for diagnosis.
red_flags: Complete vision loss or bilateral involvement — would suggest a more severe or different demyelinating process

must_ask.say: How has your vision changed, and does it hurt more when you move your eye?
Do colors, especially red, look washed out or dull in that eye?
Do you feel an electric shock down your spine when you bend your neck forward?
Have you ever had an unexplained episode of numbness or weakness before?
How many days has this vision problem been going on?

It started four days ago as mild blurring, and it has gradually become dimmer and more clouded each day.
It is only in my left eye. When I cover my left eye, my right eye sees completely fine.
The blurring and dimness have been constant and continuous for four days, not coming and going.
Everything looks foggy, especially right in the center of my field of view. Straight lines do not look wavy or distorted.
Both close-up reading and distant objects are blurry through that eye. I wear mild glasses for distance, but my prescription hasn't changed.
I don't see halos or glare around lights, though driving at night feels difficult because that eye sees everything so dimly.
No, I haven't seen any dark spots floating around, light flashes, or a curtain coming down over my eye.
No, I do not have double vision.
My eyelids are not drooping, and I have had no difficulty chewing or swallowing, even toward the end of the day.
There is an aching pain deep behind my left eyeball that shoots with sharp pain whenever I move my eyes, but the eye itself is not red.
No, I do not have tender temples, soreness in my jaw when chewing, or stiffness in my neck and shoulders.
About a year ago, my right leg went numb and tingly for three weeks before completely resolving on its own, but I have no slurred speech or dizziness today.
No, I have not bumped my head or had any injury to my eyes.
I do not have high blood pressure or diabetes, and I have never had regular diabetic eye screenings.
No, I have no history of irregular heartbeats, carotid artery problems, or blood clots.

I am not taking steroids, tuberculosis medications, hydroxychloroquine, or any medicated eye drops.
No one in my family has glaucoma, macular degeneration, or unexplained early vision loss.
Working as an accountant on spreadsheets has been very stressful and difficult, but I have not had any falls.
Yes, red objects look faded, washed out, or greyish when I view them with my left eye alone.
When I bend my chin down toward my chest, an electric shock-like sensation shoots down my spine into my legs.
I was wondering if I somehow strained my optic nerve from staring at bright computer screens for long hours at work.
I am terrified that I might go completely blind in both eyes at my age.
I was hoping to get urgent steroid eye drops and an MRI scan to check my optic nerve and brain.
Aside from that three-week episode of leg numbness a year ago and mild vitamin D deficiency, I have been healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take vitamin D3, 1,000 units once daily, and no other medications or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink socially on weekends, usually one or two glasses of wine.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable at rest, occasionally shielding her left eye when shifting gaze, and in no acute distress.
Bilateral temporal arteries are non-tender, soft, and normally pulsatile.

Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/36 in the left eye without pinhole improvement; swinging flashlight test shows a left relative afferent pupillary defect, fundoscopy reveals a normal optic disc, and left eye movement elicits retrobulbar pain.
Cranial nerves III through XII are intact with symmetric facial movement, intact facial sensation, and no ptosis.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout both upper and lower extremities.
Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception are intact and symmetric throughout all limbs.
Deep tendon reflexes are brisk 3+ at both knees and ankles, with bilateral extensor plantar responses.
Coordination tests including finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin are normal, and gait is steady with a negative Romberg test.
Passive neck flexion produces a transient electric shock sensation shooting down the spine into the legs, with no bony spinal tenderness.
Neck is supple without rigidity, and Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
